title: Fintech Fundamentals: How Digital Finance Works in Africa
subtitle: Explain, analyse and evaluate African fintech products, from payment rails and lending to remittances, and turn that knowledge into a fintech role or service.
description: An advanced, practical course on how digital payments, wallets, lending, savings and remittances really work in Nigeria and across Africa. You trace money through the rails, calculate true costs and business metrics, check licences and fraud controls, and finish with a professional case study and a 90-day plan.
outcomes: Trace a transfer through Nigeria's payment rails and explain who charges what
Explain and calculate how fintechs earn money, including fees, spreads and float
Calculate the true cost of a digital loan and a remittance and compare offers
Verify a fintech's licence and recognise fraud and Ponzi warning signs
Analyse a real African fintech with a structured case study and key metrics
Write a 90-day plan toward a specific fintech role, consultancy or venture
audience: Women who already use digital money and want to understand the fintech sector well enough to work in it, advise others or build with it.
tools: Smartphone with at least one bank or wallet app
Google Sheets or a notebook and calculator
Internet access to regulator websites (CBN, SEC, FCCPC, CAC)

modules.title: How Fintech Works: Gaps, Rails and Business Models
modules.overview: Start with the problems fintech solves in Africa, then follow a naira transfer through the real Nigerian payment rails. You finish the module able to explain how a fintech company actually earns money and where it sits on the market map.

lessons.title: The financial inclusion gap and how mobile money changed it
objectives: Define fintech and financial inclusion in precise, plain terms
Name the main barriers that kept people out of formal banking
Explain how the agent model behind mobile money removed those barriers
Separate access, usage and quality when judging inclusion

blocks.text: **Fintech** (financial technology) means using software, phones and data to deliver financial services: paying, receiving, saving, borrowing, insuring and sending money across borders. **Financial inclusion** means that people and small businesses can use useful, affordable financial services that are delivered responsibly. The word "useful" matters. An account that is opened once and never used is not inclusion; it is a statistic.

blocks.name: mobile-payments
blocks.alt: A person paying with a mobile phone
blocks.caption: For millions of Africans the first financial account was a phone wallet, not a bank account.

blocks.text: Why so many people were left out

For decades a typical bank account in much of Africa needed a branch visit, a utility bill, a reference letter, a minimum opening balance and regular monthly fees. Branches were concentrated in cities. A trader in a rural market might spend a day and the cost of transport just to deposit money. Each barrier on its own looks small. Together they made formal finance too costly for people with small, irregular incomes.

items: **Distance:** few branches outside cities, so every visit costs transport and lost trading time.
**Documents:** many adults lacked the identity papers or proof of address banks asked for.
**Cost:** minimum balances and maintenance fees eat into small savings.
**Product fit:** loans and accounts were designed for salaried workers, not market women with daily cash flows.
**Trust and literacy:** unfamiliar forms and language put people off, and some had lost money to failed institutions.

blocks.text: What mobile money did differently

Safaricom launched **M-Pesa** in Kenya in 2007. Its key idea was not the phone itself but the **agent**: a shop owner who swaps cash for electronic value and back again. A customer gives the agent cash (**cash-in**), the agent's electronic balance moves to the customer's wallet, and later the customer can send it to anyone with a phone number or take it out at another agent (**cash-out**). The bank branch was replaced by thousands of small shops. The account was opened with a SIM card and simple identity checks, and it worked on a basic phone through menus.

Nigeria followed a different path. Banks were stronger, and for years the central bank licensed mobile money mainly through banks and specialised operators rather than telecom companies. Growth came through **USSD banking codes**, bank apps, **POS agents** with card terminals at almost every junction, and app-based wallets such as Opay, PalmPay and Moniepoint. Telecom-led **Payment Service Banks** (for example MoMo PSB from MTN) were licensed later. The lesson: the same goal of inclusion can be reached through different models depending on regulation and market structure.

blocks.title: Branch banking versus agent-based mobile money
items: Branch banking
Agent-based mobile money
blocks.caption: Mobile money moved the counter from the branch to the neighbourhood shop and priced it per use.

blocks.text: Access, usage and quality

Researchers such as the World Bank's **Global Findex** survey measure whether adults own an account and whether they use it to pay, save or borrow. When you assess any fintech claim about inclusion, ask three questions. **Access:** can the person open and reach the service? **Usage:** do they actually use it regularly for things that matter to them? **Quality:** is it affordable, safe, transparent, and does it leave them better off? A loan app that reaches millions but traps borrowers in debt scores high on access and low on quality.

blocks.title: The gender gap is a design problem
blocks.text: Surveys such as Global Findex report the gap between men's and women's account ownership. Common causes are lower phone ownership among women, fewer identity documents, less control over household money and products designed without women in mind. A fintech that wants to serve women must design for these, for example by recruiting women agents and allowing simple identity tiers.

blocks.title: Worked example: what an agent changes for one trader
blocks.context: For example, Halima sells grains in a village market about 25 km from the nearest bank branch. A return bus trip costs her about ₦3,000 (approximate) and she loses half a day of sales, roughly ₦5,000 of profit on a good day.
steps: Banking her takings once a week at the branch costs her ₦3,000 + ₦5,000 = ₦8,000 per visit, about ₦32,000 in a four-week month.
A POS agent opens near the market. She now deposits to her account or wallet at the agent, paying, for example, a small agent fee of about ₦100 per deposit (agent fees vary).
Depositing three times a week costs about 3 x ₦100 = ₦300 a week, about ₦1,200 a month.
She also pays her supplier by transfer instead of carrying cash on the bus.
blocks.result: Her monthly cost of keeping money safe falls from about ₦32,000 to about ₦1,200, and she carries less cash. That saving, not the app, is the real inclusion benefit.

blocks.title: Think like an analyst
blocks.text: Whenever someone says a product "includes the unbanked", ask what barrier it removed, for whom, and at what cost to the user. A clear answer to those three points is the start of every good fintech case study.

takeaways: Fintech is technology delivering financial services; inclusion means useful, affordable, responsible use.
Distance, documents, cost, product fit and trust kept people out of banks.
The agent network, not the phone alone, made mobile money work.
Judge inclusion on access, usage and quality, not account counts.

activity.title: Map the barriers around you
steps: Pick one adult you know who rarely uses a bank (with their permission, no names needed).
Ask which of the five barriers in this lesson affect them most.
Note which financial tool they use instead (cash, ajo, wallet, POS agent).
Write two sentences on what product change would remove their biggest barrier.
activity.evidence: A short note listing the barriers, the current tool and your two-sentence product idea

lessons.title: Following a naira transfer: Nigeria's payment rails
objectives: Trace a bank or wallet transfer through NIBSS Instant Payment step by step
Explain the roles of NUBAN, BVN, NIN, switches and card schemes
Distinguish authorisation from settlement and explain where wallet float sits
Read a transfer's charges and identify who pays each one

blocks.text: Every fintech app sits on top of shared plumbing called **payment rails**: the systems, rules and institutions that move money between accounts. If you understand the rails, you can explain why one product is cheap and instant, another is slow, and why a "pending" transfer happens. This lesson follows one transfer in Nigeria from start to finish.

blocks.name: transfer-money
blocks.alt: Two people sending money between phones
blocks.caption: A transfer that feels instant on screen passes through several institutions in the background.

blocks.text: The building blocks

head: Building block
What it is
Why it matters
rows: The standard 10-digit account number used by Nigerian banks and many wallets
Lets any institution address any account in the same format
Bank Verification Number, an 11-digit biometric identity linked to a person's bank accounts, run for the banks through NIBSS
Ties accounts to one verified person for KYC and fraud control
National Identification Number from NIMC, 11 digits
Used alongside BVN for identity checks, including on wallets
Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System, owned by the CBN and banks
Runs NIP, the instant interbank transfer service, and other clearing systems
Companies such as Interswitch that route card and other transactions
Connect terminals, apps and banks; Interswitch also runs the Verve card scheme
Set the rules and fees for card payments

blocks.text: One transfer, step by step

blocks.title: How an instant transfer moves
items: Sender authorises in app
Bank debits sender
NIBSS routes the message
Receiving bank credits account
Banks settle at CBN later
blocks.caption: The customer sees the credit in seconds; the banks settle the net amounts between themselves afterwards.

items: **Name enquiry.** The sender types the 10-digit account number and chooses the bank. The app asks NIBSS to check the account and returns the account name. Always check this name before you continue; it is your main protection against sending to the wrong person.
**Authorisation.** The sender enters a PIN or uses biometrics. Her provider checks the balance, limits and fraud rules, then debits her account.
**Routing.** The instruction goes through NIP to the receiving bank or wallet provider.
**Credit.** The receiving institution credits the account and sends back a confirmation. Both customers get notifications.

**Settlement.** Banks do not move cash for each transfer. NIBSS adds up what each institution owes the others, and the net amounts are settled across their accounts at the Central Bank of Nigeria in settlement cycles.

blocks.text: That gap between the customer's instant credit and the banks' later settlement is why rails need strong rules, collateral and monitoring. It is also why a "failed but debited" transfer usually reverses automatically after checks: the debit happened, the credit did not, and the system has to reconcile it.
Where does wallet money actually sit?

When you hold ₦30,000 in a mobile money wallet, the operator does not keep it in a safe. Regulated operators must hold customers' funds, called **float**, in accounts at licensed banks, separate from the company's own money. The wallet is a record of your claim on that pool. This is why licensing and the safeguarding of float matter so much: if a company mixes customer float with its own spending, customers can lose money when it fails.

blocks.title: USSD and cards ride the same rails
blocks.text: A USSD transfer (for example dialling a bank's code such as *737# or *894#) is just a different screen for the same transfer logic. A card payment at a POS terminal goes through a switch and the card scheme for authorisation, then is settled between banks later. Same idea: message first, money settled after.
Reading the charges

Charges come from more than one place. Banks follow the CBN **Guide to Charges by Banks and Other Financial Institutions**, which sets maximum fees for electronic transfers in bands by amount. Under the version in use for several years, transfers were capped at about ₦10 up to ₦5,000, ₦25 from ₦5,001 to ₦50,000 and ₦50 above ₦50,000. Many fintechs absorb these fees or give free transfers to win customers. Separately, the government introduced a ₦50 Electronic Money Transfer Levy on qualifying receipts of ₦10,000 or more. Always check the current guide and tax rules, because both change.

blocks.title: Worked example: what a ₦20,000 transfer really costs
blocks.context: For example, Amaka in Onitsha sends ₦20,000 from her bank app to her supplier Tunde's wallet to pay for goods. Use the charge bands above as an illustration.
steps: ₦20,000 falls in the ₦5,001 to ₦50,000 band, so her bank may charge her up to ₦25 (some banks add VAT on the fee).
Amaka's account is debited ₦20,000 + ₦25 = ₦20,025.
Tunde receives ₦20,000. Because it is ₦10,000 or more, a ₦50 transfer levy may be deducted from his account, leaving ₦19,950 (if the levy applies to his account type).
Total friction on the payment is ₦25 + ₦50 = ₦75, which is 75 / 20,000 = 0.375% of the amount.
blocks.result: The transfer costs well under half of one percent and arrives in seconds, compared with taking cash across town. Knowing who pays which fee lets you explain pricing to customers clearly.

takeaways: NUBAN addresses accounts, BVN and NIN verify people, NIBSS runs the instant rail.
Customers are credited instantly; banks settle net positions at the CBN later.
Wallet balances are claims on float that must be held at licensed banks.
Always confirm the name returned by name enquiry before sending.

activity.title: Trace and price one of your transfers
steps: Open your bank or wallet app and find a recent transfer you sent.
Write down the amount, the fee charged and the time it took.
Mark each step from this lesson that happened (name enquiry, authorisation, credit).
Check whether the recipient paid any levy and calculate the total cost as a percentage.
activity.evidence: A one-page note or screenshot (with account numbers covered) showing the steps and your cost calculation

lessons.title: How fintechs make money and the African market map
objectives: List the main revenue models used by African fintechs
Calculate a merchant's payment fee from a published pricing rule
Place companies on a market map by customer and job
Explain why unit economics decide which fintechs survive

blocks.text: A fintech is a business. Free transfers and cashback attract customers, but the company must eventually earn more per customer than it spends to serve them. If you can explain where a company's money comes from, you understand most of its strategy.

blocks.name: money-with-wings
blocks.caption: Every naira that moves through a fintech can carry a small fee, a spread or a float return.

blocks.text: The main revenue models

head: Model
How it earns
Typical example
rows: A flat or percentage fee per payment
Payment gateways charging merchants for card payments
Fee split between provider and agent on cash-out
Lending at a higher rate than the cost of funds
Interest earned on customer balances held at banks, where rules allow
Difference between the rate given and the market rate
A slice of the card fee paid by merchants

blocks.text: Most successful companies combine several. A wallet may make little on free transfers but earn on bill payments, cards, loans and float. When you study a company, list every revenue line you can see in its app and pricing pages.
Why so many transfers are free

Free transfers are a **customer acquisition** tool. The provider pays the interbank fee itself because a customer who moves her daily money through the app is likely to buy airtime, pay electricity bills, use a debit card or take a loan there. Each of those carries a commission or margin. Money that sits in wallets also adds to float. So the free product is the door, and the paid products are the rooms behind it. When a fintech starts charging for transfers, it usually means the paid products did not earn enough on their own.

Agent networks work the same way. A POS agent typically charges the customer a cash-out fee, while the provider charges the agent a smaller fee per transaction and sells the agent the terminal or rents it out. Both earn only if the agent has enough daily volume, which is why providers compete hard for busy locations such as markets, motor parks and campuses.

blocks.title: Worked example: a merchant's gateway fees
blocks.context: For example, Chioma sells skincare online and uses a gateway whose published Nigerian pricing (at the time of writing, check the current page) is 1.5% + ₦100 per local transaction, with the ₦100 waived below ₦2,500 and the total fee capped at ₦2,000.
steps: Order of ₦2,000: 1.5% x 2,000 = ₦30. The ₦100 is waived, so the fee is ₦30.
Order of ₦10,000: 1.5% x 10,000 = ₦150, plus ₦100 = ₦250, which is 2.5% of the order.
Order of ₦200,000: 1.5% x 200,000 = ₦3,000, plus ₦100 = ₦3,100, but the cap applies, so the fee is ₦2,000 (1% of the order).
In a month with 60 orders of ₦10,000, she pays 60 x ₦250 = ₦15,000 on ₦600,000 of sales.
blocks.result: Her effective fee is 2.5% on mid-sized orders, lower on small and very large ones. She can now price products knowing the true payment cost, and the gateway earns ₦15,000 from her month.

blocks.text: The market map
Analysts group companies by who the customer is and what job the product does. The map below is a simple way to place any company quickly. Many large players sit in more than one box.

blocks.title: A simple fintech market map
items: Consumer wallets and transfers
Merchant payments and gateways
Consumer savings, credit, insurance
SME credit and business banking
blocks.caption: Top row moves money, bottom row stores or lends it; left serves individuals, right serves businesses.

items: **Mobile money and wallets:** M-Pesa (Kenya), MTN MoMo (several countries), Wave (Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire), Opay and PalmPay (Nigeria).
**Merchant payments and infrastructure:** Paystack (bought by Stripe in 2020), Flutterwave, Interswitch.
**Agent banking and SME banking:** Moniepoint, with large POS agent networks.
**Digital banks and lenders:** Kuda, Carbon, FairMoney.
**Savings and investment apps:** PiggyVest, Cowrywise.
**Cross-border and remittances:** Chipper Cash, LemFi, plus long-standing money transfer operators.

blocks.title: Names change fast
blocks.text: Fintech companies merge, change licences, enter new countries or close. Treat this list as a starting point and confirm each company's current status on its own website and with the relevant regulator before you quote it.
Unit economics in one paragraph

**Unit economics** compare what one customer brings in with what it costs to win and serve them. A company that pays ₦1,000 in referral bonuses to win a user who earns it ₦50 a month needs 20 months just to recover the bonus, before staff, fraud losses and data costs. This is why many fintechs that grew fast on free services later added fees or closed. When you read about a company's growth, ask about revenue per active user and the cost to acquire one. Module 3 shows you how to calculate both.

takeaways: Fintech revenue comes from fees, spreads, float, interest and software.
Calculate real fees from the published rule, including caps and waivers.
Place companies on a map: who they serve and whether they move or grow money.
Growth without healthy unit economics does not last.

activity.title: Build a mini market map
steps: Draw the four-box market map on paper or in Google Sheets.
Place at least eight fintech products you know or use in the boxes.
For three of them, write their main revenue model from the table.
Check one company's public pricing page and calculate the fee on a ₦15,000 payment.
activity.evidence: A photo or file of your market map with revenue notes and one fee calculation

quiz.q: A fintech reports 5 million accounts opened, but only 400,000 used in the last 30 days. Which inclusion dimension is weakest?
quiz.explain: Accounts show access. Only 8% are active, so usage is the weak point.

quiz.q: Before confirming a transfer, what protects the sender most against paying the wrong person?
options: Checking the account name returned by name enquiry
Using USSD instead of the app
quiz.explain: Name enquiry returns the registered account name; checking it catches wrong numbers and many scams.

quiz.q: Where should a regulated wallet operator keep customers' balances?
options: As float in accounts at licensed banks, separate from company funds
quiz.explain: Customer float must be safeguarded at licensed banks and kept apart from the company's own money.

quiz.q: Using the pricing 1.5% + ₦100 (₦100 waived below ₦2,500, cap ₦2,000), what is the fee on a ₦6,000 order?
quiz.explain: 1.5% of 6,000 is ₦90, plus ₦100 because the order is above ₦2,500, giving ₦190.

quiz.q: In the NIP flow, what happens at settlement?
options: Banks pay net amounts owed to each other through their CBN accounts
The receiving bank shows the account name
quiz.explain: Customers are credited instantly; banks settle net positions later at the central bank.

quiz.q: A company earns money mainly from the gap between the exchange rate it gives customers and the market rate. Which revenue model is this?
quiz.explain: The difference between the customer rate and market rate is an FX spread, common in remittances.

modules.title: Products in Depth: Lending, Savings, Remittances and Risk
modules.overview: Go inside the products that matter most to households and small businesses: digital loans, savings and investment apps, and cross-border transfers. You learn to calculate their true cost, check who regulates them, and spot the fraud and consumer risks every fintech must manage.

lessons.title: Digital lending: credit scoring, true cost and responsible rules
objectives: Explain how digital lenders decide whom to lend to using traditional and alternative data
Convert a flat loan fee into a monthly and annualised rate
Name the Nigerian bodies that oversee digital lenders and credit data
Identify predatory lending practices and the rights borrowers have

blocks.text: Digital lending means loans applied for, approved and paid out through an app, USSD or website, often in minutes. It grew because banks rarely lent small amounts to people without payslips or collateral. The promise is real: a trader can restock today instead of next month. The risk is also real: some apps charged very high fees and harassed borrowers. An advanced fintech learner must understand both the machinery and the rules.

blocks.name: personal-finance
blocks.alt: A person reviewing personal finances on a screen
blocks.caption: A digital loan decision is made from data in seconds, so the data and the rules behind it matter.

blocks.text: How the credit decision is made

blocks.title: Inside a digital loan decision
items: Verify identity (BVN, NIN)
Pull bureau and account data
Score repayment risk
Set limit, price, term
Disburse and collect
blocks.caption: Each step uses data; weak identity checks or careless scoring show up later as fraud or bad loans.

blocks.text: **Traditional data** comes from credit bureaus. In Nigeria, licensed private credit bureaus include CRC Credit Bureau, FirstCentral Credit Bureau and CreditRegistry, and the CBN runs its own Credit Risk Management System for banks. Lenders report who borrowed and whether they repaid. **Alternative data** includes bank or wallet transaction history (how much flows in each month and how regular it is), bill payments and, for business loans, POS sales. A lender looking at a POS agent's six months of steady takings can lend to her even without a payslip.

Alternative data has limits. A woman whose income passes through her husband's account, or who trades mostly in cash, can look like a poor risk even when she is reliable. Scoring models built on one group's history can also treat other groups unfairly. Good lenders test their models for this, offer ways to add income evidence, and explain decisions in plain language when they decline someone.

The **score** estimates the chance a borrower will repay. From it the lender sets a **limit** (often small at first, rising after good repayment), a **price** and a **term**. Good lenders start small and grow with the customer. This is called graduated lending and it protects both sides.
Working out the true cost

Loan apps often show a fee or a total to repay rather than an annual rate. To compare loans fairly, turn everything into a rate for the same period. The **monthly rate** is the total cost divided by the amount borrowed, adjusted to 30 days. The simple **annualised rate** multiplies that by the number of periods in a year. Lenders are expected to disclose the full cost before you accept, including all fees.

blocks.title: Worked example: comparing two loan offers
blocks.context: For example, Bisi runs a phone accessories stall in Ibadan and needs ₦50,000 for stock. App A offers 30 days, repay ₦57,500. App B offers 3 months, repay ₦62,000 in total.
steps: App A annualised (simple): 15% x 365 / 30 = about 182.5% a year.

App B cost: ₦62,000 - ₦50,000 = ₦12,000 over 3 months, which is 24% in total or about 8% a month (a simple estimate; because she repays some principal each month, the true rate on what she still owes is higher).
Her stock turns over in about 3 weeks with a 20% gross margin, so ₦50,000 of stock earns about ₦10,000 per cycle.
blocks.result: App A's ₦7,500 cost eats 75% of one cycle's ₦10,000 profit. App B's cost is lower per month and gives her several stock cycles. The cheaper-looking short loan is the more expensive one.

blocks.text: Who regulates digital lending in Nigeria

items: **CBN:** licenses banks and microfinance banks that lend, and sets credit reporting rules.

**FCCPC (Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission):** registers and supervises digital and non-traditional consumer lenders. It introduced an interim framework in 2022 and later full regulations for digital, electronic, online or non-traditional consumer lending. It publishes the list of approved lenders.
**NDPC (Nigeria Data Protection Commission):** enforces the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, which covers how lenders collect and use phone contacts and personal data.
**State money-lending laws** also apply to some lenders, so licence status varies by business type.

blocks.title: Red flags of a predatory loan app
blocks.text: Demands access to your contacts or photos; threatens to message your family or employer (debt shaming, which regulators have prohibited); hides the total repayment until after disbursement; is not on the FCCPC approved list; pressures you to take a new loan to repay the old one. A responsible lender does none of these.

blocks.title: Borrower rights to know
blocks.text: You are entitled to clear terms before you accept, to know the total amount payable, to complain to the lender and then to the FCCPC, and to have your data handled lawfully. Lenders also report to credit bureaus, so repaying on time builds a credit history that can unlock cheaper loans.

takeaways: Lenders score risk from bureau data plus alternative data such as transaction history.
Convert every loan to a monthly and annualised rate before comparing.
FCCPC supervises digital consumer lenders; NDPC enforces data protection.
Contact harvesting and debt shaming are signs of a predatory app.

activity.title: Audit a real loan offer
steps: Open a loan app or a bank's loan page and note one offer's amount, term and total repayable (do not accept it).
Calculate the monthly and simple annualised rate.
Check whether the lender appears on the FCCPC approved digital lenders list.
List which phone permissions the app asks for and judge whether each is necessary.
activity.evidence: A short audit sheet with the offer, your rate calculation, the FCCPC check result and the permissions list

lessons.title: Savings, investment apps and cross-border remittances
objectives: Distinguish a savings wallet, a bank deposit and an investment product
Check the regulator and protection behind a savings or investment app
Calculate the total cost of a remittance including the exchange-rate margin
Choose the cheaper of two remittance offers using total amount received

blocks.text: Savings and remittance products touch two of the most important money flows in African households: putting money aside for the future and receiving support from relatives abroad. Both are full of fine print. This lesson teaches you to read it.

blocks.name: savings
blocks.alt: A person adding coins to savings
blocks.caption: Before you save in an app, know whether it is a deposit, a wallet or an investment.

blocks.text: Three things that look alike but are not

head: Product
What you own
Who regulates
Main protection
rows: A deposit at a licensed bank
NDIC deposit insurance up to a limit
A claim on float held at banks
Float safeguarding rules; NDIC pass-through cover for mobile money subscribers, check current limits
Investment product (for example a money market fund)
Units in a fund or a security
Fund rules, custodians and trustees; value can go up or down

blocks.text: Savings apps often combine these. An app may hold your money in a partner bank, or invest it in a mutual fund managed by an SEC-registered fund manager. Read the terms to find out which. The words "guaranteed returns" on an investment product are a warning sign: real investments carry risk, and only insured deposits have a formal guarantee, and only up to the insured limit.

blocks.title: Check the limit yourself
blocks.text: NDIC sets maximum insured amounts per depositor that differ by type of institution, and it has raised them over time. Look up the current figures on the NDIC website rather than relying on an old article.
How savings apps are designed to change behaviour

Digital savings products borrow ideas from traditional ajo and esusu groups and add automation. Common features are **automatic debits** (a fixed amount taken from a card or account daily, weekly or monthly), **locked savings** that pay a higher rate but charge a fee or forfeit interest if broken early, **goal savings** with a target and date, and **group savings** where members save toward a shared target. These features work because they make saving the default and spending the effort. When you analyse a savings app, ask what behaviour it encourages, what it charges for early withdrawal, and who holds the money.

Returns should also be compared honestly. An app paying 12% a year when inflation is higher still leaves the saver with less buying power, although she is better off than holding cash at zero. A product description that hides this is not lying, but a good adviser will explain it.
How remittances work and what they cost

A **remittance** is money a migrant sends home. Licensed **International Money Transfer Operators (IMTOs)** and newer app-based companies collect money in one currency, convert it, and pay out in naira or another local currency to a bank account, wallet or cash agent. The sender pays in two ways: an upfront **fee**, and an **exchange-rate margin**, which is the gap between the rate you get and the mid-market rate. The margin is often bigger than the fee and is easy to miss.

Global development goals (UN Sustainable Development Goal target 10.c) aim to cut remittance costs below 3% and remove corridors costing more than 5%. The World Bank's **Remittance Prices Worldwide** database compares providers on many corridors, and sending money to Sub-Saharan Africa has long been among the most expensive in the world.

blocks.title: Two ways a remittance can charge you
items: Visible fee
Hidden FX margin
blocks.caption: Always add both parts together, or simply compare how much the recipient finally gets.

blocks.title: Worked example: which offer delivers more naira?
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi in Manchester sends £200 to her mother in Enugu. Assume a mid-market rate of ₦2,000 per £1 (illustrative only).
steps: Provider A advertises "zero fees" and a rate of ₦1,940. Her mother receives 200 x 1,940 = ₦388,000.
A's cost: mid-market value of £200 is ₦400,000. Cost = ₦400,000 - ₦388,000 = ₦12,000, which is 3% of the amount.
Provider B charges a £3 fee and gives a rate of ₦1,990. Ngozi pays £203; her mother receives 200 x 1,990 = ₦398,000.
B's cost: £203 is worth ₦406,000 at mid-market. Cost = ₦406,000 - ₦398,000 = ₦8,000, which is about 1.97%.
blocks.result: Provider B, with a visible fee, delivers ₦10,000 more and costs about 2% against A's 3%. "Zero fees" is not the same as cheapest.

blocks.text: Payout options also affect cost and convenience. Bank or wallet payout is usually cheapest and fastest. Cash pickup at an agent costs more but serves relatives without accounts. Some providers pay out in foreign currency into a domiciliary account, which avoids conversion at the sending end but may cost more to withdraw. Always compare like with like: same amount, same payout method, same day.

blocks.title: Use licensed channels only
blocks.text: Unlicensed informal channels and social media "forex sellers" may offer better rates but carry fraud and legal risk. Check that the provider is licensed in the sending country and, for Nigeria payouts, works with a CBN-licensed IMTO or bank.

takeaways: Deposits, wallet balances and investments carry different protections.
NDIC insures deposits up to a limit; investments are regulated by SEC and can lose value.
Remittance cost = fee + exchange-rate margin.
Compare providers by what the recipient finally receives.

activity.title: Compare two remittance quotes
steps: Pick a corridor that matters to you or your community (for example UK to Nigeria).
Get live quotes for the same amount from two licensed providers' websites or apps.
Note the fee, the rate and the amount received, and find the mid-market rate on a reputable converter.
Calculate each provider's total cost as a percentage and decide which is cheaper.
activity.evidence: A small table with both quotes, the mid-market rate and your cost calculation

lessons.title: Fraud, KYC and consumer protection in digital finance
objectives: Explain tiered KYC and why limits rise with stronger identity checks
Describe the main fraud types in African digital finance and how each works
List the controls a provider and a customer should use against them
Handle a fraud complaint through the right escalation path

blocks.text: Trust is the product. If customers fear losing money, they go back to cash. Every serious fintech invests heavily in identity checks, fraud monitoring and complaint handling, and regulators judge companies on them. Anyone who works in or advises fintech needs to speak this language.

blocks.name: shield
blocks.caption: KYC, monitoring and customer education together form the shield around digital money.

blocks.text: Know Your Customer, in tiers

**KYC (Know Your Customer)** means verifying who a customer is before and while serving them. It supports **AML/CFT** rules (anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism). The CBN uses a **three-tiered KYC** framework. Low tiers can be opened with basic details and have low transaction and balance limits, which supports inclusion. Higher tiers need BVN or NIN verification, address checks and more documents, and allow higher limits. The trade-off is deliberate: easy entry for small amounts, stronger checks for larger risk. Check the current limits in CBN circulars, as they are revised.
The fraud types you must recognise

head: Fraud type
How it works
Key control
rows: Fraudster tricks or bribes a way into a new SIM on the victim's number, then receives OTPs and resets banking
Telecom checks, bank alerts on SIM change, app device binding
Caller pretends to be the bank or a customer service agent and asks for PIN, OTP or BVN
Customer education: banks never ask for PIN or OTP
Stolen passwords or phones used to log in and transfer
Strong PIN, biometrics, device binding, transaction limits
Accounts rented or opened to receive and move stolen money
KYC, monitoring unusual inflows, quick freezing and reporting
Promise high fixed returns, pay early members from new deposits, then collapse
Licence checks with SEC or CBN, investor education

blocks.title: Five controls every provider needs
items: Tiered KYC with BVN or NIN
Device binding and strong authentication
Real-time transaction monitoring
Fast freeze and reversal process
Clear complaint and refund channel
blocks.caption: Missing any one of these leaves a gap fraudsters will find.

blocks.text: How a provider's fraud team works

Inside a fintech, fraud control is a loop, not a single tool. **Rules** flag risky patterns, for example a new device followed by a large transfer to a never-used beneficiary within minutes, or many small inflows to one account from different people. **Analysts** review flagged cases, contact customers and decide whether to release, hold or block. **Feedback** from confirmed fraud updates the rules. Too strict, and genuine customers are blocked and leave; too loose, and losses grow. Balancing the two is a daily judgement, and it is a large source of jobs in the sector. Teams also track fraud losses as a share of transaction value and the time taken to resolve each case, so they can see whether controls are improving month by month.

items: **Cooling-off periods:** some providers delay or limit large transfers right after a new device login or PIN reset.
**Beneficiary checks:** warnings when sending to an account reported for fraud or newly opened.
**Agent monitoring:** watching for agents who split transactions or overcharge customers.
**Customer education:** in-app messages that remind users the provider never asks for OTPs.

blocks.text: Data protection is consumer protection

Fintechs hold sensitive data: identity numbers, faces, transaction histories, contacts. The **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023** requires a lawful basis for processing, collecting only what is necessary, keeping it secure and reporting serious breaches to the Nigeria Data Protection Commission. A product team that asks "do we really need this permission?" is doing both compliance and good design.

blocks.title: Worked example: handling a reported fraud
blocks.context: For example, Kemi calls a wallet's support line at 9:10 am. She received a call from "the bank", read out an OTP, and ₦85,000 left her wallet to an account at another bank at 9:02 am.
steps: The agent verifies Kemi's identity and immediately blocks her wallet to stop further debits.
The fraud team logs the case and sends a request through the interbank channel for the receiving bank to place a hold on the beneficiary account.
Because she reported within minutes, there is a better chance the money is still in the receiving account; the team records the time and reference numbers.
Kemi is told to file a police report, to keep all reference numbers, and given a written complaint reference with an expected response time.
If unsatisfied with the outcome, she can escalate to the CBN's consumer protection department or the FCCPC as applicable.
blocks.result: Speed is everything: the first minutes decide whether funds can be frozen. A clear internal process and a calm, well-briefed customer give the best chance of recovery.

blocks.title: The rule every customer should hear
blocks.text: No genuine bank, wallet or regulator will ever ask for your PIN, password or OTP by call, SMS or WhatsApp. If anyone does, end the call and contact your provider through the number in its official app.

takeaways: Tiered KYC balances easy access with stronger checks for higher limits.
SIM swap, social engineering, account takeover, mules and Ponzi schemes are the core fraud types.
Controls: KYC, device binding, monitoring, fast freezes and clear complaints.
The NDPA 2023 makes data minimisation and security a legal duty.

activity.title: Fraud-proof one app you use
steps: Open a bank or wallet app you use and find its security settings.
Turn on biometric login, transaction PIN and alerts if they are off.
Find the official fraud reporting number or in-app channel and save it in your contacts.
Write a three-line WhatsApp message warning your family about OTP scams, in your own words.
activity.evidence: A checklist of settings enabled, the saved fraud contact and your warning message

quiz.q: A loan app lends ₦40,000 for 30 days and asks for ₦46,000 back. What is the simple annualised rate?
quiz.explain: Cost ₦6,000 is 15% for 30 days; 15% x 365/30 is about 182.5% a year.

quiz.q: A loan app asks for permission to read all your contacts and photos. What is the best judgement?
options: A red flag for debt shaming and data misuse; check FCCPC approval
Only a problem for business loans
quiz.explain: Contact harvesting is linked to debt shaming. Responsible lenders do not need it, and FCCPC keeps an approved list.

quiz.q: Which body regulates a money market fund offered inside a savings app?
quiz.explain: Collective investment schemes such as money market funds fall under SEC Nigeria.

quiz.q: Provider X: no fee, rate ₦1,950 per £. Provider Y: £2 fee, rate ₦1,995 per £. Sending £100 with mid-market ₦2,000, which delivers more naira?
options: X, because it has no fee
quiz.explain: X pays out 100 x 1,950 = ₦195,000. Y pays out 100 x 1,995 = ₦199,500. Y delivers more even after the £2 fee.

quiz.q: Why does tiered KYC allow low-tier accounts with only basic details?
options: Because BVN is no longer used
To support inclusion while limiting risk through low transaction limits
quiz.explain: Low tiers make access easy but cap amounts; stronger checks unlock higher limits.

quiz.q: A customer reports an OTP scam five minutes after the debit. What should the provider do first?
options: Block her account and request a hold on the beneficiary account immediately
Tell her to call the police only
Reverse the money from company funds without checks
quiz.explain: Speed matters: stop further loss and try to freeze the funds before they move on.

modules.title: Analysing Fintech Companies and Planning Your Path
modules.overview: Turn what you know into professional work: a structured case study of a real company, the metrics investors and managers use to judge it, and a 90-day plan toward a fintech role, consultancy or venture.

lessons.title: Researching a fintech company: the case-study method and due diligence
objectives: Apply an eight-part framework to study any fintech company
Verify a company's licence and registration with the right regulator
Spot the warning signs of a fake platform or Ponzi scheme
Write focused discovery questions for a fintech client or employer

blocks.text: Whether you want a job at a fintech, want to consult for one, or want to use one in your own business, you need to understand a company quickly and accurately. Analysts use a repeatable method so they do not miss anything important. This lesson gives you that method and the checks that keep you away from fakes.

blocks.name: researching
blocks.alt: A person researching documents and information
blocks.caption: A good case study is built from checkable sources, not excitement on social media.

blocks.text: The eight-part case-study framework

head: Part
Question to answer
Where to look
rows: What barrier or pain does it remove, for whom?
Consumers, merchants, SMEs, agents? Which segment?
What exactly can a user do, step by step?
Use the app yourself, help centre
Which banks, switches, schemes or networks does it rely on?
Which licence, from whom, in which countries?
Who else solves the same problem and how is this different?
Access, usage, quality; fraud, credit and conduct risks

blocks.title: From first look to finished case study
items: Use the product yourself
Read pricing and terms
Verify licences
Compare with competitors
Write findings and risks
blocks.caption: Hands-on use first, then documents, then verification, then judgement.

blocks.text: Verifying licences: the step most people skip

items: **Payments, wallets, banks, microfinance banks, PSBs, IMTOs:** the CBN publishes lists of licensed institutions on its website.
**Investment platforms, fund managers, crowdfunding:** check SEC Nigeria's registered operators.
**Digital consumer lenders:** check the FCCPC approved list.
**Company existence and directors:** search the CAC public register.
**Other countries:** use that country's central bank or financial regulator, for example the Central Bank of Kenya for Kenyan payment service providers.

blocks.text: Using the product yourself

Reading about a fintech is not the same as using it. Open a basic account and record each screen of onboarding: what identity it asks for, how long verification takes, and what you can do before full KYC. Make one small real action, such as buying ₦100 of airtime or sending ₦200 to yourself. Note the fees shown, the confirmation messages and how easy it is to find help. Then read app store reviews from the last three months, sorting by most recent, and group complaints into themes such as failed transfers, slow support or unexpected charges. These first-hand notes often reveal more than a press release, and they give you concrete examples to quote in interviews and reports.

Note the exact licence type. A company that says it is "licensed by the CBN" may hold a switching licence, a mobile money licence, or simply partner with a licensed bank. Each brings different obligations and different protection for customers. Also check for enforcement news: regulators sometimes publish sanctions, suspensions or warnings, and a recent penalty is an important part of any honest case study.

blocks.title: Ponzi warning signs
blocks.text: Fixed high returns such as 20% or more a month; returns paid mainly from new members' money; rewards for recruiting others; no clear product or revenue; pressure to reinvest; vague or no SEC registration. Nigeria saw the MMM scheme freeze withdrawals in late 2016, and similar schemes have appeared since. Any "fintech" fitting this pattern is not a fintech to study as a model; it is a risk to warn people about.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 30-minute licence and model check
blocks.context: For example, Funmi is preparing for an interview at a savings app and wants to understand it before she arrives.
steps: She downloads the app, opens a basic account and notes the products: flexible savings, locked savings and a dollar fund.
From the terms she finds that savings are held with a named partner bank and the dollar fund is managed by a named fund manager.
She checks the fund manager on SEC Nigeria's register and the bank on the CBN list; both appear.
She reads the pricing page: no account fee, a withdrawal fee on early break of locked savings, and fund management fees inside the fund.
She writes: "Revenue likely comes from early-withdrawal fees, fund management fees and interest margin on pooled savings."
blocks.result: In half an hour Funmi has a verified, specific picture of the business and three intelligent interview questions about growth, fees and customer protection.

blocks.text: Discovery questions that show real understanding

items: Which customer segment drives most of your active users today, and which do you want next?
What share of revenue comes from transactions versus lending or float?
What is your biggest fraud pattern right now and how do you detect it?
How do you measure whether customers are better off, not just active?

takeaways: Use the eight-part framework so nothing important is missed.
Always verify the exact licence with the right regulator.
High fixed returns plus recruitment rewards signal a Ponzi scheme.
Specific discovery questions show genuine sector knowledge.

activity.title: Start your capstone company file
steps: Choose one African fintech company for your capstone.
Use its product for at least one real or test action (for example opening a basic account).
Fill in parts 1 to 6 of the framework table with sources for each answer.
Verify its licence on the correct regulator's website and record the exact licence type.
activity.evidence: A completed framework table for parts 1 to 6 with a screenshot or link proving the licence check

lessons.title: Measuring a fintech: growth, unit economics and inclusion metrics
objectives: Calculate active-user rate, take rate, CAC and payback period
Calculate a non-performing loan ratio and explain what it signals
Read headline figures critically and ask for the missing denominator
Choose inclusion metrics that show customers are better off

blocks.text: Fintech press releases are full of big numbers: millions of users, billions in transactions. Professionals turn those into a few ratios that show whether the business is healthy and whether customers benefit. Learn these and you will read any fintech report with confidence.

blocks.name: growth-analytics
blocks.caption: Big totals impress; ratios tell you whether a fintech is healthy.

blocks.text: The core metrics

head: Metric
Formula
What it tells you
rows: Users who transacted in last 30 days / registered users
Whether people actually use the product
Sum of all payment amounts processed in a period
Scale of money moving through the platform
How much the company earns per naira processed
Marketing and incentive spend / new active customers
Cost to win one real customer
CAC / monthly gross profit per customer
Months to recover the cost of a customer
Loans overdue 90+ days / total loan book

blocks.title: From sign-ups to better-off customers
items: Registered accounts
Verified (KYC done)
Active in last 30 days
Using several products
Measurably better off
blocks.caption: Each level is smaller than the one below; strong fintechs push more users up the pyramid.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a wallet's quarterly numbers
blocks.context: For example, a wallet company (illustrative figures) reports 1,000,000 registered users, 280,000 active in the last 30 days, ₦2 billion monthly TPV and ₦16 million monthly revenue. It spent ₦6 million on referral bonuses and ads last month and gained 12,000 new active users. Gross profit per active user is ₦40 a month.
steps: CAC: ₦6,000,000 / 12,000 = ₦500 per new active user.
Payback: ₦500 / ₦40 = 12.5 months.
Its small loan book is ₦500 million, with ₦45 million overdue more than 90 days: NPL ratio = 45 / 500 = 9%.
blocks.result: The headline "1 million users" hides that only 28% are active and each new customer takes over a year to pay back. A 9% NPL ratio suggests lending needs tighter scoring. These three ratios are the questions to ask management.

blocks.text: What each ratio is telling you

A **low active rate** usually means onboarding incentives brought in people who had no real need, or that the product failed them early. A **falling take rate** can be healthy (the company is winning large merchants who pay lower percentages) or worrying (competition is forcing prices down). A **long payback period** is acceptable only if customers stay for years and the company has enough cash to wait. A **rising NPL ratio** often shows up months after a lender relaxed its scoring to grow faster, so watch the trend, not one figure.

Ratios also connect. If a company raises fees, take rate rises, but active users may fall. If it cuts referral bonuses, CAC drops, but so may growth. Good analysis looks at several ratios together and over several periods, ideally at least four quarters, before drawing a conclusion.
Reading numbers critically

items: **Ask for the denominator.** "500,000 loans" means little without the default rate and average size.
**Check the period.** Annual TPV and monthly TPV differ twelvefold; some reports mix them.
**Registered is not active.** Prefer 30-day or 90-day active figures.
**Look for the source.** Audited accounts, regulator data or surveys such as Global Findex and the GSMA State of the Industry Report on Mobile Money are stronger than press releases.

blocks.text: Inclusion metrics that matter

Inclusion-focused investors and development partners ask whether customers are better off. Useful measures include the share of active users who are women, first-time account holders or rural; average cost per transaction as a share of the amount; complaint resolution time; share of borrowers who repay without distress and then qualify for larger, cheaper loans; and savings balances held over time. These numbers are harder to collect than downloads, which is exactly why a fintech that tracks them stands out.

Where a company publishes nothing, you can still build evidence. Short customer interviews (ten users is enough to spot patterns), a count of agents in one market, or a comparison of fees across three competitors are all legitimate primary research. State your method and sample size clearly so readers know how much weight the findings can carry, and never present a small sample as if it represented the whole country.

blocks.title: Build a one-page scorecard
blocks.text: For your capstone company, collect any of these metrics that are public, note the source and date beside each, and mark the ones you could not find. Saying "not disclosed" honestly is more professional than guessing.

takeaways: Active rate, take rate, CAC, payback and NPL ratio summarise a fintech's health.
Always ask for the denominator and the time period.
Registered users flatter; active users inform.
Inclusion metrics show whether customers end up better off.

activity.title: Build your company scorecard
steps: Search your capstone company's website, reports and reliable news for published figures.
Fill a scorecard with any of the six core metrics you can find, with source and date.
Calculate at least one ratio yourself from figures given (for example active rate).
Add two inclusion metrics you would ask the company for if you could interview them.
activity.evidence: A one-page scorecard in Google Sheets or on paper with sources and your calculation

lessons.title: Fintech careers, consulting and your 90-day plan
objectives: Match fintech roles to your existing skills and experience
Position your sector knowledge in a CV, profile or service offer
Price a small fintech-related consulting project with a clear scope
Write a realistic 90-day plan toward one specific opportunity

blocks.text: Fintech companies employ far more than software engineers. They need people who understand customers, agents, compliance, risk, operations and communication, especially people who understand how women and small traders really handle money. Your lived experience plus this course's knowledge is a genuine advantage.

blocks.name: interview
blocks.alt: Two people in a job interview
blocks.caption: Sector knowledge you can explain with examples is what sets you apart in a fintech interview.

blocks.text: Roles and what they need

head: Role
What the work involves
Skills that transfer
rows: Resolving complaints, fraud reports, failed transfers
Recruiting, training and supporting POS or mobile money agents
Checking identity, monitoring transactions, regulator reporting
Spotting patterns, setting rules, investigating cases
Deciding what to build, improving onboarding, campaigns
Training customers, working with NGOs and cooperatives

blocks.text: Positioning yourself

Replace general statements like "passionate about fintech" with proof. On a CV or LinkedIn profile, write lines such as "Analysed a Nigerian wallet's revenue model, licence and active-user rate (case study linked)" or "Trained 30 market women to use wallet savings safely, with an OTP-scam module". Link your capstone. For consulting, offer a narrow, useful service: for example, helping cooperatives choose and set up a collections wallet, or reviewing a small fintech's help-centre content for clarity and scam warnings.

Interviewers in fintech often test judgement with scenarios: "A customer says money left her account but she did not send it. What do you do?" or "Our agents in one state have twice the complaints of others. How would you investigate?" Prepare by practising answers using what you learned in Module 2: secure the account, gather facts and reference numbers, check patterns, escalate, and follow up. A calm, step-by-step answer shows you understand both the customer and the controls.
Building credibility on a small budget

items: **Write in public:** one short post a fortnight explaining a fintech concept from this course in plain language, such as how to compare remittance costs.
**Join communities:** fintech and women-in-tech groups on LinkedIn and WhatsApp, and attend free webinars from regulators and industry bodies when announced.
**Volunteer your skills:** run a free scam-awareness session at a church, mosque, cooperative or market association and record the attendance.
**Keep a dated portfolio:** case study, scorecard, training materials and any feedback received.

blocks.title: Worked example: pricing a small consulting job
blocks.context: For example, Adaeze is asked by a cooperative of 120 members to recommend a digital collections tool and train its executives. She estimates her own rate at ₦15,000 per working day (her figure, based on local rates she has checked).
steps: Scope: compare three licensed options, one site visit, a written recommendation, and a 2-hour training for 8 executives.
Time: research 1.5 days, visit 0.5 day, report 1 day, training preparation and delivery 1 day = 4 days.
Fee: 4 x ₦15,000 = ₦60,000, plus transport about ₦8,000 (approximate) = ₦68,000.
She writes what is excluded: no account opening on members' behalf, no handling of members' money, and extra sessions at ₦15,000 each.
She asks for 50% upfront and 50% on delivery of the report.
blocks.result: A clear scope, a defensible fee of ₦68,000 and written exclusions protect both Adaeze and the cooperative, and keep her away from touching client funds.

blocks.title: Never hold other people's money
blocks.text: As an adviser or trainer, do not collect, keep or transfer clients' or members' funds, and never ask for their PINs or OTPs. Handling customer money is a regulated activity and the fastest way to lose trust.
Your 90-day plan

blocks.title: A 90-day fintech plan
items: Days 1-30: finish case study
Days 31-60: publish and network
Days 61-90: apply or pitch
Day 90: review and adjust
blocks.caption: Each month ends with something you can show, not just something you read.

items: **Name one target.** For example: "agent network officer at a Lagos-based payments company" or "financial literacy partner for two cooperatives in Enugu".
**Days 1 to 30:** complete your capstone case study and scorecard; use two products in your target category every week.
**Days 31 to 60:** share a short summary of your case study on LinkedIn or WhatsApp status; contact five people working in your target area with one specific question each.
**Days 61 to 90:** send at least five tailored applications or two consulting proposals, each referring to your case study.
**Day 90:** count results (replies, interviews, clients), note what worked, and set the next 90 days.

blocks.title: Stay current
blocks.text: Regulations and companies change monthly. Follow the CBN, SEC, FCCPC and NDPC websites for circulars, and read company announcements directly. Note the date of every fact you use.

takeaways: Fintech needs operations, compliance, risk, product and training skills, not only engineers.
Show proof of sector knowledge: case studies and specific results.
Scope and price consulting clearly, and never handle client money.
A 90-day plan with one target and monthly outputs turns learning into opportunity.

activity.title: Draft your 90-day plan
steps: Write your single target opportunity in one sentence.
Pick the role from the table closest to it and list three of your transferable skills.
Fill in the three 30-day blocks with dated, specific actions.
Rewrite one line of your CV or profile to show fintech proof instead of interest.
activity.evidence: A one-page 90-day plan and your rewritten CV or profile line

quiz.q: A company says it is "licensed by the CBN". What should an analyst do next?
options: Find the exact licence type on the CBN's published list
quiz.explain: Licences differ (switching, mobile money, bank, partner arrangement), each with different obligations. Verify the exact type.

quiz.q: A platform promises 25% monthly returns and bonuses for recruiting friends. What does this most likely indicate?
quiz.explain: High fixed returns plus recruitment rewards are classic Ponzi warning signs.

quiz.q: A wallet has ₦3 billion monthly TPV and ₦21 million monthly revenue. What is its take rate?
CAC is ₦800 and monthly gross profit per customer is ₦50. What is the payback period?
quiz.explain: ₦800 / ₦50 = 16 months to recover the cost of acquiring a customer.

quiz.q: A loan book is ₦200 million and ₦24 million is overdue 90+ days. What is the NPL ratio?
As a consultant helping a cooperative choose a wallet, which action should Adaeze refuse?
options: Collecting members' contributions into her own account
quiz.explain: Handling clients' money is regulated and risky; advisers should never hold it.

finalQuiz.q: Which change made mobile money work for people far from bank branches?
options: A network of local cash-in and cash-out agents
finalQuiz.explain: Agents replaced the branch counter, letting people convert cash and e-money close to home.

finalQuiz.q: On Nigeria's instant transfer rail, which system routes the transfer message between institutions?
finalQuiz.explain: NIBSS runs NIP, which routes interbank instant transfers; settlement happens afterwards at the CBN.

finalQuiz.q: What is a wallet balance, legally and practically?
options: A claim on customer float held at licensed banks
A share in the fintech company
finalQuiz.explain: Operators must safeguard customer float at licensed banks; the wallet records your claim on it.

finalQuiz.q: Using 1.5% + ₦100 (₦100 waived below ₦2,500, cap ₦2,000), what is the fee on ₦150,000?
finalQuiz.explain: 1.5% of 150,000 is ₦2,250, plus ₦100 is ₦2,350, but the ₦2,000 cap applies.

finalQuiz.q: A lender asks ₦69,000 back on ₦60,000 after 30 days. What is the monthly rate?
Which Nigerian body keeps the approved list of digital consumer lenders?
finalQuiz.explain: The FCCPC registers and supervises digital and non-traditional consumer lenders.

finalQuiz.q: A remittance shows "zero fees". What must you still check?
options: The exchange-rate margin against the mid-market rate
finalQuiz.explain: The FX margin is a hidden cost that is often larger than a visible fee.

finalQuiz.q: A caller from "your bank" asks for the OTP just sent to you. What is the correct response?
options: End the call and contact the bank through its official app
finalQuiz.explain: Genuine providers never ask for PINs or OTPs; this is social engineering.

finalQuiz.q: Why do higher KYC tiers allow higher limits?
options: Because the CBN dislikes small accounts
Stronger identity checks reduce money laundering and fraud risk
finalQuiz.explain: Tiered KYC matches limits to the strength of identity verification.

finalQuiz.q: A wallet has 2,000,000 registered and 500,000 active users. What is the 30-day active rate?
Which part of the case-study framework asks which banks, switches or schemes a company depends on?
finalQuiz.explain: Rails and partners covers the infrastructure the product runs on.

options: One named target, a finished case study by day 30, outreach by day 60, applications by day 90
finalQuiz.explain: A single target with monthly outputs you can show turns learning into results.

capstone.title: African Fintech Deep-Dive Research Project
capstone.brief: Produce a professional case study of one African fintech company (business model, rails, licence, market position, metrics and inclusion impact), a one-page overview of the market category it competes in, and a 90-day plan naming your specific target opportunity in the sector.
steps: Choose one company and use its product yourself for at least one action.
Complete all eight parts of the case-study framework with a source and date for each answer.
Verify its exact licence on the right regulator's website and record the licence type.
Build a metrics scorecard: active rate, take rate, CAC, NPL or any figures disclosed, marking gaps honestly.
Write a one-page category overview: main players on the market map, revenue models and two current trends you can source.
Assess inclusion impact on access, usage and quality, and name the top two risks for customers.
Finish with your 90-day plan toward one named opportunity.
evidence: Case study covering all eight framework parts with dated sources
Screenshot or link proving the licence check
Metrics scorecard with at least one ratio you calculated
One-page category overview with a market map
Dated 90-day plan with one named target

sources.title: Central Bank of Nigeria (licensed institutions, guidelines, circulars)
Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System (NIBSS): NIP and BVN
Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (digital lending)
GSMA State of the Industry Report on Mobile Money
